evals.prompt: We run PipelineDays Rotterdam, a one-day community DevOps conference, 320 attendees, CFP-driven, six volunteer organizers. The budget is finished and signed off: EUR 41,000 of expenses, and we agreed sponsorship covers 78% of that with ticket sales covering the rest. The venue floor fits 8 sponsor tables. Our program policy is that no talk slot is ever for sale. Give us the sponsor rate card for the 2027 edition.
evals.expected_output: A rate card that starts from a computed revenue target (~EUR 32,000), then a 3-tier ladder inside the community top:floor band, gated on the four physical axes, with no purchasable stage time and no exclusivity line, a hard booth floor, independently priced add-ons, and a signing deadline a quarter out.
expectations: Computes the revenue target as 78% of EUR 41,000 (approximately EUR 32,000) and states it is the sum the whole card must raise
Refuses to divide the revenue target evenly across the tiers, stating that cost-recovery sets the sum and not the shape of the ladder
Recommends three tiers as the default ladder shape for this event
Sets a top-tier to floor-tier price ratio inside the community range of roughly 2:1 to 7.5:1, near 4-5:1
Gates the tiers on ticket allotment, floor presence, stage time and branding prominence, and on no other axes
Removes purchasable stage time from the sellable inventory because the program policy forbids selling talk slots
Prices no track or category exclusivity, deleting the line rather than parking it for later
Starts table/floor presence at a hard tier, with no cheaper route onto the floor beneath that tier
Treats the per-tier ticket allotment as a subtractable cost component rather than free swag
Presents the top tier first as the anchor and makes the middle tier the visibly best value
Prices named branded surfaces (such as lanyards, coffee or the evening event) independently of the tier ladder
Sets the sponsor signing deadline roughly a fiscal quarter before the event date

evals.prompt: I'm setting sponsorship prices for RustPorto, our first conference, about 250 people, and our total budget is EUR 26,000. The only prospectus I could actually get hold of is from a large US foundation conference. Their tiers run $160,000 / $99,000 / $65,000 / $33,500 / $16,750 / $11,500 / $4,250 / $1,750, booths start at the $11,500 tier, and passes are counted at $899 each. How do I use their card to build ours?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to carry the foundation dollar figures across scale, a transposition of ratios and structures only, a community-scale top:floor band, a 2-4 tier recommendation, and a target derived from the EUR 26,000 budget rather than from the comp.
expectations: Refuses to carry the foundation-scale dollar figures onto the community-scale card
Identifies the comp's roughly 91:1 top-to-floor spread as a foundation-scale artifact that does not transpose to a 250-person event
Prescribes a community-scale top:floor band of roughly 2:1 to 7.5:1, modal near 4-5:1
Transposes structures rather than prices, naming at least the booth price floor, stage time confined to a capped top tier, struck-through sold-out surfaces, and a contact-us line
Warns that a foundation-scale booth floor can exceed a community event's entire revenue target
Derives the card's total from the EUR 26,000 budget and its sponsorship share, not from the comp's numbers
Recommends gathering comparable cards from same-community, same-region, same-scale events
Requires every comparable price to carry a date, treating an undated price as unusable
Recommends 2 to 4 tiers with three modal, rather than mirroring the comp's eight tiers
Carries the per-pass value across as a per-unit cost line inside each tier
Sequences the methods: cost-recovery fixes the total, market-comp bands each tier, value-based allocates within the band

evals.prompt: Two offers landed for InfraSummit Lisbon, our 400-person infrastructure conference. A cloud vendor will give us $45,000 of platform credits, which is their published list price, and they want the Platinum spot that we sell at $9,000. We'd never buy their product otherwise, we run everything on donated hardware from the university. They said they could add $2,000 cash on top if it helps. Separately, a catering company offered to cover lunch for free, which is a $4,200 line in our budget. What do I give each of them?
evals.expected_output: Credits valued at the budget line they displace (near zero), catering valued at $4,200, Platinum refused for the credits, the top tier kept cash-only, and both deals written into the agreement at displaced-cost value with delivery terms.
expectations: Values the cloud credits at the budget line they displace rather than at the $45,000 list price
Concludes the credits displace nothing or near-nothing because the event would never have paid for that product this edition
Refuses to grant the Platinum tier in exchange for the credits
Values the catering donation at the $4,200 budget line it displaces
Grants tier placement at the displaced-cost value, treating it the same as cash of that amount
Keeps the top tier cash-only or cash-majority
Justifies the cash-only top tier by the fixed costs that must be paid in cash, such as venue deposits, insurance or catering minimums
Rejects retail-value and equivalent-media-value framing as a valuation method
For the mixed offer, counts the $2,000 as cash and the credits at displaced cost, and gates the tier on the cash share
Requires the displaced-cost figure, the deliverable and the delivery date to be written into the sponsor agreement
Requires the agreement to state the remedy if the in-kind delivery fails, treating an undelivered in-kind commitment as a breach rather than a discount

evals.prompt: Three of us run KubeDay Tallinn, a one-day event for about 180 people. We're all volunteers and none of us has ever sold anything in our lives. I was going to put "sponsorship packages available, contact us" on the site so we can size each deal to whatever the company can afford. The event is in 11 weeks. Does that work?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation against quote-gating at single-event volunteer scale, a published short ladder instead, the quote-gated rung deleted rather than demoted, contact-us lines reserved for custom or sold-out slots, and the budget prerequisite stated.
expectations: Recommends against quote-gating the whole card for this event
Gives as the reason that an unpriced card at single-event scale stalls every deal behind organizer availability and reads as having something to hide
Deletes the quote-gated rung outright given zero sales capacity, rather than demoting it to a lower-ranked option
States that quote-gating is legitimate at portfolio or network scale, selling annual reach to sophisticated repeat buyers
Recommends a published ladder with printed prices
Recommends a shorter, simpler ladder of two or three tiers rather than finer segmentation, given the 11-week runway
Notes that sponsors sign roughly a fiscal quarter ahead, making an 11-week window tight against sponsor budget cycles
Reserves contact-us lines for genuinely custom slots or slots that have sold out, not for the whole card
Names no-ladder-by-design as a legitimate architecture tied to a free-to-attend, donation and stand-fee funding model, and says whether it applies here
Requires an expense total and a sponsorship share to exist before any tier price is set
Specifies that any early-bird is a dated price on the card rather than a percentage-off banner

evals.prompt: Our biggest sponsor for the last three editions of FrontendCamp Lyon just emailed. They'll re-up at Gold, which is on our card at $6,000, but they want 15% off for loyalty and they want an answer today. Our sponsorship lead wants to just say yes to lock it in before they go quiet. What do we tell them?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the loyalty discount with the compounding-anchor reason, the ROI report and next edition's early-bird offered instead, price protection or right of first refusal named as the published alternatives, a list of what is genuinely negotiable, and the approval and logging rules.
expectations: Refuses the 15% loyalty discount and states a returning-sponsor discount is not a rate-card feature at any scale
Gives as the reason that a loyalty discount compounds and permanently anchors every future negotiation with the event's most visible sponsor
Offers the post-event ROI report and the relationship as the renewal lever instead of a rate cut
Offers next edition's early-bird date as the concrete alternative on price
Names price protection (locking the current rate ahead of an increase) or a right of first refusal on the same tier as the published alternatives to a discount
Lists payment schedule changes, split invoices or cross-fiscal-year timing as negotiable
Lists equal-value benefit swaps as negotiable
Lists bundling add-ons into the tier at the sum of their card prices as negotiable, framed as convenience rather than a discount
States the person closing the deal cannot approve a deviation alone, and requires a named approver or a two-person rule
Prefers adding benefit value at displaced cost over cutting the published number
Requires any granted deviation to be logged with sponsor, tier, what moved, why and who approved
Warns that sponsors in the same community compare notes and one leaked concession reprices next year's whole ladder

evals.prompt: Post-mortem numbers from ReactConf Manchester, 500 attendees. Platinum was $12,000 with 2 slots and sold out in nine days. Gold at $7,500 sold zero, we ran the event with an empty Gold tier. Silver at $3,000 filled all six slots. The lanyard sponsorship at $4,000 sold out on day one, so we've pulled it off the page for next year to keep the card tidy. Our sponsorship target was $62,000 and we closed $47,000. What do we change for next edition?
evals.expected_output: Platinum and the lanyard both repriced upward, the empty Gold diagnosed as a benefit-gating failure rather than a price problem, the sold-out add-on kept visible and struck through, and the $15,000 shortfall split between price, ladder and pipeline causes.
expectations: Reads the nine-day Platinum sellout as evidence the top tier was under-priced and raises Platinum for the next edition
Does not recommend lowering the Platinum price
Diagnoses the empty Gold tier as a step-up that buys no visible benefit jump, not only as a price problem
Prescribes re-gating Gold on the four benefit axes so the step-up from Silver is visible
Raises the lanyard add-on price next edition because it sold out
Does not lower the lanyard add-on price
Rejects removing the sold-out lanyard from the published card and instead strikes it through, leaving it visible
Justifies keeping it visible as live scarcity plus social proof for the surfaces still available
Treats each sellout as the repricing signal for next edition rather than a cleanup task
Splits the $15,000 shortfall between price, ladder and pipeline causes before changing any number
Routes the pipeline half of the shortfall to sponsor outreach work rather than assuming a pricing fix
Does not invent an industry benchmark sell-through, close or pass rate to judge the result against

evals.prompt: Sanity check on our draft card before it goes live for DataWorks Summit, our own vendor-run user conference, 900 attendees. Tiers: Platinum $8,000 / Gold $4,500 / Silver $2,000. Add-ons: Lanyards $5,000, Coffee cart $2,500, Happy Hour $4,000. Our designer also proposed a $1,200 "Exhibitor Only" line that gets a shared table but no logo anywhere, so smaller companies can still get on the floor. And a $3,000 "Lightning Talk" add-on, five minutes on the main stage, for anyone who missed Platinum. Anything wrong here?
evals.expected_output: The lanyard add-on approved despite out-pricing Gold, the Exhibitor Only line rejected as a breach of the booth price floor, and the Lightning Talk add-on rejected as re-selling Platinum's gated stage time below the tier that gates it.
expectations: Approves the $5,000 lanyard add-on out-pricing the $4,500 Gold tier as legitimate practice
States that a named branded surface may out-price a mid tier without cannibalizing the ladder
Rejects the $1,200 Exhibitor Only line as a cheap route onto the floor beneath the booth price floor
States that floor presence must begin at a hard tier, with nothing cheaper granting it
Rejects the $3,000 Lightning Talk add-on because it re-sells stage time gated at Platinum for less than Platinum
Defines cannibalization precisely as an add-on re-selling a tier's core gated benefit (floor presence or stage time) below the tier that gates it
Offers the alternative of pricing a stage-time add-on above the cheapest tier that includes stage time, or not selling it at all
Confirms stage time is sellable inventory here because the event sits at the vendor-run pole
Keeps the remaining add-ons priced independently of the tier ladder
Caps scarce add-on inventory visibly on the card
Does not recommend lowering the lanyard price so it sits below the Gold tier

evals.prompt: HackNantes is a free two-day hackathon, 220 hackers, no tickets at all, sponsors fund everything. Costs land around $38,000. My co-organizer drew up six sponsor tiers at $500 / $1,500 / $3,000 / $6,000 / $10,000 / $18,000 so there's an entry point for every company budget. We also want a free tier for the local Python user group who run workshops for us, and we figured that's a nice way to warm them up to a paid tier next year. Review this for me.
evals.expected_output: The ladder cut to at most four tiers with the surplus rungs named as price gaps, the target set at the full $38,000, the sequence collapsed to cost-recovery, and the free community tier kept as a reserved non-commercial category rather than an upsell funnel.
expectations: Cuts the ladder to at most four tiers
States that five or more tiers is one tier too many at any scale
Names the surplus rungs as price gaps wearing a persona costume rather than real sponsor segments
Allows a fourth tier only when a genuinely distinct sponsor persona exists, never to fill a price gap
Sets the revenue target at effectively 100% of the $38,000 expense total because there is no ticket revenue line
Collapses the price-setting sequence to cost-recovery for this free-to-attend event
States that value-based work here decides which sponsor gets which tier, not where the prices sit
Keeps the free community tier as a permanently reserved category for non-commercial local organizations
Explicitly rejects using the free community tier as an upsell or freemium funnel into paid tiers
Defines the free tier's benefits as logo plus a ticket, with no table and no pitch
States that the floor tier's job is entry and social proof rather than revenue

evals.prompt: I run sponsorship for a three-event series under one brand, vendor-backed: a 2,000-person flagship conference plus two regional 400-person days. The board wants it done properly this year and has asked for a willingness-to-pay study across our sponsor base before we set the 2027 numbers. We also want to sell exclusivity on our new AI track, and two sponsors have asked about signing for all three events in one contract. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: The willingness-to-pay study refused in favour of published comparable cards, the method sequence stated, track exclusivity priced at a multiple above the top general tier with a hard cap, and the multi-event bundle priced as a small fixed published step.
expectations: Rejects a willingness-to-pay survey method such as Van Westendorp or MaxDiff as unworkable at one event's sponsor-pool size
Names comparable events' published rate cards as the practical substitute for willingness-to-pay research
Sequences the methods as cost-recovery for the total, market-comp to band each tier, value-based to allocate within the band
States that cost-recovery needs the budget's expense total and sponsorship share before any tier is priced
Prices the AI track exclusivity at a multiple above the top general tier rather than at add-on money
Puts a hard cap on the number of exclusivity slots sold
Confirms exclusivity is sellable here because the series sits at the vendor or foundation pole
Prices the three-event bundle as a small fixed published discount step in the single-digit percent range, scaling with the number of events signed
States that bundling requires real portfolio contract mechanics to honour, and that this is why it is promoted here
Promotes value-based pricing for the AI track because no comparable event publishes a price for that inventory
Does not list track exclusivity as an add-on beside surfaces like coffee or lanyards
Does not offer an open-ended or negotiated discount in exchange for the three-event commitment

evals.prompt: Our sponsor card for GoConf Valencia carries a 20% early-bird banner on all three tiers, running until slots sell out. Event is May 14. Two sponsors missed the March 1 cut-off and are asking us to honour the rate anyway, and one of them is a $9,000 deal we really want. What's the right call, and how should we run the early-bird next year?
evals.expected_output: Both extension requests refused, the percentage banner replaced by a dated price on the top tier only, the cut-off timed to sponsor budget lock-in a quarter out, and any exception routed through the named approver and the deviation log.
expectations: Refuses to extend the early-bird rate for either sponsor
States that a deadline extended once is no longer a deadline
Replaces the percentage-off banner with a dated price printed on the card
Restricts the early-bird to the top tier only
Sets the early-bird cut-off to catch sponsor budget lock-in roughly a fiscal quarter before the May 14 event
Notes that an 'until slots sell out' early-bird is not a calendar deadline and cannot pull deals forward
States the early-bird's purpose is pulling the largest deals forward at near-zero effort
Rejects granting the $9,000 sponsor an off-card exception on the grounds of deal size
Requires any approved exception to go through the named approver and be recorded in the deviation log
Warns that the first exception becomes the market price because sponsors talk to each other
